intro: The New Testament is short. Its 27 books fit in the back quarter of most Bibles. Yet they were written across a huge world, from Jerusalem to Rome, in a time of Roman rule, Jewish debate and long sea voyages. This unit reads those books inside that world. It asks who ruled, who argued, who traveled and who wrote.

You will read the four Gospels as four portraits of one teacher, alike and different. You will follow the book of Acts from a Jerusalem festival to a Roman prison. You will read letters as letters, with senders, receivers and reasons. You will open Revelation and learn how an apocalypse works. And you will trace how these books, and not others, became a canon.

Throughout, the course describes and attributes. It says what the text says and what Christians, Jews, Muslims and scholars have made of it. It does not say who is right. By the end you will be able to name each kind of writing, place it in its time, and explain how two readers can read the same page differently.
bigQuestion: How does knowing the Roman and Jewish world of the first century change the way you read the New Testament?

timeline.t: Rome takes control of Judea and the surrounding region
Herod the Great dies; Rome divides his kingdom among his sons
Pontius Pilate becomes Roman governor of Judea
Jesus's public teaching and death in Jerusalem, as most scholars date them
Paul writes 1 Thessalonians, usually called the oldest New Testament book
Paul in Corinth while Gallio is proconsul, the firmest date in his life
Roman armies destroy the Temple in Jerusalem
The Gospel of Mark, most scholars think, is written
Matthew and Luke, with Acts, are written around this time
Revelation and the Gospel of John, in most scholars' dating
Marcion proposes a short canon; churches begin to state their own lists
Athanasius's Easter letter lists exactly today's 27 New Testament books

words.d: "good news"; the message about Jesus and the name of the four books that tell his story
"seen together"; Matthew, Mark and Luke, which share many stories, order and wording
Jewish teachers who applied the Torah to daily life; ancestors of rabbinic Judaism, many scholars say
a group tied to the Temple priests; the Gospels say they did not believe in resurrection
a short story from daily life that carries a bigger point and makes the listener think
from Latin for suffering; the part of each Gospel that tells Jesus's arrest, trial and death
rising from the dead; Christians believe God raised Jesus on the third day
"one who is sent"; the closest followers of Jesus, and Paul
a letter; the New Testament letters follow the shape of ordinary Greek letters
a person who is not Jewish; in Acts and Paul's letters, Gentiles join the movement
"unveiling"; writing that uses visions and symbols to speak hope in a hard time, like Daniel and Revelation
the list of books a tradition accepts as scripture; the New Testament canon has 27 books

test.q: Which Roman official do all four Gospels say sentenced Jesus?
test.why: Pilate, governor of Judea c. 26–36 CE, gives the sentence in every Gospel.

test.q: Which group in the Gospels was linked to the Temple priests?
test.why: The Sadducees were the priestly party; the Essenes lived apart and the Zealots resisted Rome.

test.q: Where were the Dead Sea Scrolls found?
test.why: The scrolls came from caves near Qumran, by the Dead Sea, starting in 1947.

test.q: Which Gospel do most scholars think was written first?
test.why: Mark is dated c. 65–75 CE, and Matthew and Luke appear to use it as a source.

test.q: Which Gospel has long "I am" speeches and seven signs?
test.why: John stands apart from the Synoptics with discourses, "I am" sayings and seven signs.

test.q: In the parable of the Good Samaritan, who passes by the injured man?
choices: A tax collector and a soldier
test.why: Luke 10 says a priest and a Levite pass by before the Samaritan stops.

test.q: Which set of blessings opens the Sermon on the Mount?
test.why: Matthew 5 opens with the Beatitudes, each beginning "Blessed are."

test.q: What does this course say about whether the resurrection happened?
choices: It describes what Christians believe and leaves the truth question to faith
test.why: The course attributes beliefs, notes other traditions' views, and does not rule on the claim.

test.q: Which book continues the Gospel of Luke?
test.why: Acts opens by recalling its "former treatise" to Theophilus, the same person Luke addresses.

test.q: Where was Paul's base for his journeys?
test.why: Acts 13 sends Paul out from Antioch in Syria, and he returns there between journeys.

test.q: How are Paul's letters arranged in the New Testament?
test.why: Romans, the longest, is first and Philemon, the shortest, is last; churches come before persons.

test.q: What does Paul ask Philemon to do?
test.why: Philemon 16 asks that Onesimus be received no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother; it does not say more.

test.q: Which Hebrew Bible book is most like Revelation in kind?
test.why: Daniel and Revelation are both apocalypses, using visions and symbols in a time of pressure.

test.q: What does "Babylon" stand for in Revelation, most readers agree?
test.why: Revelation borrows the name of the city that destroyed the first Temple for the empire of its own day, Rome.

test.q: Whose 367 CE letter first lists exactly the 27 books of the New Testament?
test.why: Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, gave the first surviving list matching today's New Testament.

write.prompt: How does a New Testament writer use the shape of a genre to make a point? Choose either a Gospel scene (for example Matthew 22:15–22 or Luke 10:25–37), a letter (Philemon 1–25 or 1 Corinthians 13), or a vision (Revelation 21:1–4). Cite two or three passages by book, chapter and verse. Explain what the text says, how its genre works, and how at least two kinds of readers have read it.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verse every time you cite the text.
Attribute every belief: "Christians believe," "Jewish tradition reads," "many scholars think."
Compare readings; do not judge which is true.
Use the unit's terms: gospel, Synoptic, parable, Passion, epistle, apocalypse, canon.
Say what the text leaves unsaid as well as what it says.
